activities.caption: fill the blanks — the two numbers that seal the promise
activities.name: linRolesCloze

config.text: A linear function is a promise: equal steps in x buy equal steps in y, always. Two numbers seal the promise: %%0%%, how steep, and %%1%%, where it starts.
config.hint: One letter for steepness, one for the starting point.

activities.caption: two temperature scales, one line — drag the divider
activities.name: linConvCompare

config.prompt: Two temperature scales, one line — drag the divider:

before.label: Celsius
before.text: 0 at freezing, 100 at boiling — water's own scale

after.label: Fahrenheit
after.text: 32 at freezing, 212 at boiling — reached by F = 1.8·C + 32

config.why: The 1.8 is the slope (nine Fahrenheit degrees per five Celsius degrees) and the 32 is the intercept — where Fahrenheit's scale happens to put zero.

activities.anchor: A journey graph's gradient is speed
activities.caption: gradient or intercept — file each reading
activities.name: linRoleSort

config.prompt: File each reading under the number it describes:

items.label: the rate — how much y changes per one step of x
the taxi's base fare, paid before moving
the 'flag falls' value of the story

config.why: Two lines can share an intercept and mean completely different things — only the gradient tells you which ordering scales worse.

config.prompt: From (1, 3) to (4, 12): the rise is 9 and the run is 3. What is the gradient?
config.why: m = 9 ÷ 3 = 3 — and any other pair of points on the line gives the same 3. That sameness is what makes it a line.
config.context: on a curve this ratio changes as you move along

config.prompt: Rebuild the line through (2, 1) and (6, 9) — what comes first:
config.why: The slope fixes the direction, the anchor fixes the position — two points determine a line completely because a line owns nothing more.

activities.caption: bet before you read on — the perpendicular partner
activities.name: linPerpPredict

config.q: The perpendicular partner of m = 3 has gradient…
choices: ⅓ — the reciprocal keeps the sign
config.why: A perpendicular turns the direction through 90°, which swaps the rise and run and flips a sign: rise 3 for run 1 becomes rise −1 for run 3.

activities.anchor: The distance between two points comes from
activities.caption: find the backwards claim — reading the grid
activities.name: linDistSpot

config.prompt: One of these coordinate claims is backwards — click it:
lines: The distance between (1, 2) and (4, 6) comes from Pythagoras: gaps 3 and 4, so d = 5.
Proving a right angle on the grid means checking that the gradients multiply to −1.
A steeper line is always the bigger quantity.
config.correction: A steeper gradient means a faster rate of change, not a larger value — which line wins depends on the x-range you care about.
config.why: Graphs are read with their axes, not admired in the abstract.

config.root: Tote bags: a £500 rig plus £9 of materials per bag, selling at £15 — break-even at x ≈ 83.3. You raise the price to £18. What happens to break-even?

start.text: Which way does the crossing move?

choices.label: Slides left — the steeper revenue line meets cost sooner
choices.feedback: Correct: 500 + 9x = 18x crosses at x ≈ 55.6 instead of 83.3 — each bag now contributes £9 instead of £6 toward the fixed £500.

choices.label: Slides right — a higher price needs more sales
choices.feedback: The crossing moves left, not right: the per-bag contribution grew, so the fixed cost is cleared faster.

choices.label: Unchanged — the fixed cost dominates
choices.feedback: The fixed cost sets the height of the hurdle, but the per-bag contribution sets how fast you clear it.

left.text: Same two-line diagram, every decision in the model.

right.text: Read the geometry honestly: steeper revenue meets the same cost line sooner.

fixed.text: Negotiate materials to £8 and the cost line flattens — also moving break-even down.

config.why: Two crossing linear models make the break-even point, and their difference is itself linear — which is why 'linear model' is the first phrase in every business analytics course.
